summary: Specifies a profile of the ACE framework that uses OSCORE for communication security and for proof of possession of a key bound to an OAuth 2.0 access token. The key is owned by the client. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A permission slip is tied to a secret key and messages are protected end to end with it.

questions: how does ace oscore derive master salt
subtitle: How a small device proves it holds an OAuth access token's key and sets up OSCORE-protected CoAP with a server.

tldr.problem: Constrained devices need to be authorized to use a resource and need a secure channel to it, without carrying many libraries or running heavy handshakes.
tldr.mechanism: The authorization server issues an access token bound to a symmetric key. The client and resource server swap two nonces, build an OSCORE security context from the key, and prove possession of the key by the first protected exchange.
tldr.outcome: The coap_oscore profile gives authorization, a secure channel and key possession proof in one scheme on top of the ACE framework. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9203 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on the ACE framework in RFC 9200 and on OSCORE in RFC 8613.

sections.title: What the coap_oscore Profile Is
sections.content:
This document specifies the coap_oscore profile of the ACE framework (RFC 9200). A client (C) and a resource server (RS) talk using the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252). The client uses an access token bound to a symmetric key, the proof-of-possession (PoP) key, to authorize its access.

The symmetric secret is used as input material for keying material derivation. To get communication security and PoP, client and server use OSCORE (RFC 8613). PoP is not a dedicated protocol element: it occurs after the first message exchange using OSCORE.

OSCORE uses COSE to secure CoAP messages and can also secure HTTP, so a similar profile using HTTP could be specified analogously. The RFC assumes that a given resource on an RS is associated to a unique authorization server (AS).
sections.eli5: A small gadget wants to use a service. It shows a permission slip and then talks in a private code that only the gadget and the service can work out.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The RS keeps a collection of OSCORE security contexts with associated authorization information (policy) for each client. The flow has four steps.

  1. The client asks the AS's token endpoint for an access token for the resource it wants. This exchange MUST be confidentiality protected and authentic. OSCORE is RECOMMENDED, but TLS or DTLS MAY be used instead.
  2. The client generates a nonce N1 and its own OSCORE Recipient ID ID1, and posts the token, N1 and ID1 to the RS's authz-info endpoint with Content-Format application/ace+cbor. This endpoint is not protected, except when updating access rights.
  3. If the token is valid, the RS answers 2.01 (Created) with a nonce N2 and its own Recipient ID ID2.
  4. Both sides concatenate the input salt, N1 and N2 into the OSCORE Master Salt and derive the complete security context. The client then sends an OSCORE-protected request.

The security context lives until the token is deleted, for example by expiration. It is discarded when a token is used to derive a new context for that client.
sections.eli5: First you get a permission slip. Then you and the shop each pick a random number and swap them. Mixing those with the secret code gives you a private way to talk.

sections.title: Talking to the AS and the OSCORE Input Material
sections.content:
The client posts to the token endpoint as in RFC 9200. To update access rights without changing an existing context, it MUST include a req_cnf object whose kid carries the identifier of the OSCORE Input Material. The AS MUST check that this identifies a key it previously issued to that client, or else decline with invalid_request.

The AS can signal that OSCORE is REQUIRED by returning ace_profile with the value coap_oscore. It MUST send a Master Secret and an identifier of the OSCORE Input Material. It MAY also send a context identifier, an AEAD algorithm, an HKDF algorithm, a salt and the OSCORE version number. These travel in the osc field of the cnf parameter.

The OSCORE_Input_Material is a CBOR map (or JSON object) with all parameters optional:

  • id (label 0), version (1), ms (2), hkdf (3), alg (4), salt (5), contextId (6)

The same parameters MUST appear in the token's claims, and the Master Secret MUST be encrypted so only the RS can read it. A CWT protected with COSE_Encrypt or COSE_Encrypt0 is RECOMMENDED. The AS MUST send different input material, and so different tokens, to different clients.
sections.eli5: The permission slip comes with a secret code and a few settings, all sealed so only the shop can open them. Every visitor gets a different code.

sections.title: Client and RS Exchange: Nonces and Setup
sections.content:
The client MUST generate N1, a nonce very unlikely to have been used before with the same input keying material. A 64-bit random number is RECOMMENDED. It also picks ID1 so it does not collide with its other Recipient IDs. It wraps the token, N1 (nonce1, CBOR key 40) and ID1 (ace_client_recipientid, key 43) in a CBOR map and posts it to authz-info.

The RS validates the token. If the token carries claims it cannot process, a mandatory parameter is missing, or the osc field has unrecognized parameters, it MUST answer with an error equivalent to 4.00 (Bad Request). Otherwise it generates N2 and ID2, makes sure ID2 differs from the client's ID, and replies 2.01 (Created) with nonce2 (key 42) and ace_server_recipientid (key 44).

Both sides then set Master Salt = salt | N1 | N2, where | is byte string concatenation. With JSON, each piece is prefixed by its size in one byte, the result is base64 encoded, and nonces and salt are at most 255 bytes. Each side sets its Sender ID to the other's Recipient ID, takes the Master Secret and any AEAD, HKDF, ID Context and version from the AS data, and defaults from RFC 8613 when omitted.

A client MUST stop and MUST NOT derive the context if a parameter is missing or if the two recipient IDs are equal.
sections.eli5: You and the shop each shout a random number. Both numbers get stirred into the secret code the same way, so you each end up with the same private key without ever saying it out loud.

sections.title: Using, Updating and Discarding the Context
sections.content:
Once the context exists, the RS verifies each OSCORE request. If that succeeds and the resource needs authorization, the RS looks up the authorization information of the token tied to the context and checks that it covers the resource and action. After the token expires the RS MUST NOT use the context and MUST answer requests with an unprotected 4.01 (Unauthorized).

To update access rights, the client posts the new token to authz-info protected with the existing OSCORE context, sending only the access_token field. The RS checks that the token's kid matches the input material identifier of the context, replaces the old token and replies 2.01 (Created) with no payload, or 4.01 (Unauthorized) on failure.

The client MUST discard the context when the sequence number space ends, the token becomes invalid, it gets a number of 4.01 responses (the number is set by the application), or it receives a new nonce while reposting a non-expired token. The RS MUST discard it when the sequence number space ends, the token expires, or the client replaces the context by posting a token to the unprotected authz-info endpoint. Messages in flight under the old context may fail verification, and CoAP observations registered earlier may need to be cancelled.
sections.eli5: When your slip changes, you hand in a new one using the private talk already set up. If the slip runs out or the numbering runs out, you throw away the old code and start again.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The framework's and OSCORE's security considerations apply. Proof of possession here means both parties establish the same context, so both the OSCORE request and response pass verification. RS authentication needs the client to trust the AS and the OSCORE response to verify.

The nonces guarantee unique AEAD keys and nonces, so they MUST NOT be reused with the same input keying material, even after reboots. A 64-bit random nonce is RECOMMENDED. The RFC says that, considering the birthday paradox, the average collision for each nonce happens after 2^32 messages. A counter is risky if state can be lost, because an on-path attacker can replay a client message to force reuse of an old N1.

It is RECOMMENDED that the RS keep a single token per client. If one OSCORE Input Material is shared across several RSs, those servers can impersonate the client or each other. Basic OSCORE is meant for point-to-point use, not multicast or publish-subscribe.

On privacy, the token and nonces are sent in the clear to authz-info. A client reusing one token across servers can be tracked by its value, even if the token is encrypted. Random nonces are better than counters, which may leak information. OSCORE identifiers can also reveal or correlate clients, and message sizes and addresses still leak after OSCORE is set up.
sections.eli5: The random numbers must never repeat, or someone could trick you into using an old lock. Also, anything shouted out loud, like your slip, can be used to recognize you.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the coap_oscore profile in the ACE Profiles registry with CBOR value 2. It also registered four OAuth parameters (nonce1, nonce2, ace_client_recipientid, ace_server_recipientid) with CBOR keys 40, 42, 43 and 44, each of type bstr.

IANA also created the "OSCORE Security Context Parameters" registry, initially populated with the parameters in the OSCORE Input Material table. The RFC also registers the osc confirmation method in the CWT and JWT Confirmation Methods registries and gives guidance to the designated experts.
sections.eli5: The names and numbers used by this scheme were written into official lists so nobody else uses them for something different.
